record.original_question: For k-orbit polytopes with k ≥ 3, define the right analogue of the chirality group: a group-theoretic invariant that measures how far the polytope is from being regular and behaves well despite the fact that different flag stabilizers may have different normalizers.

evidence.quote: Problem 7. Determine the “correct” way to generalize the chirality group to k-orbit polytopes.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ (with a minimum and a maximum element) whose elements (called faces) are ranked from $-1$ to $n$, every maximal chain (called a flag) contains exactly one face of each rank, $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected, and the diamond condition holds: for any two faces $F<G$ of ranks differing by $2$ there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. The diamond condition implies that for each flag $\Phi$ and each $i\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ there is a unique flag $\Phi^i$ differing from $\Phi$ only in its rank-$i$ face. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts freely on flags; $\mathcal{P}$ is called a $k$-orbit polytope when this action has exactly $k$ orbits. The polytope is regular iff $k=1$, in which case $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ is generated by involutions $\rho_0,\dots,\rho_{n-1}$ subject to a string Coxeter-type presentation. For a $2$-orbit chiral polytope, the chirality group is defined as follows: let $W$ be the abstract string $C$-group with the regular presentation, and let $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ be presented as a quotient of the orientation-preserving subgroup $W^+\le W$ by a normal subgroup $M\trianglelefteq W^+$; the chirality group is then $X(\mathcal{P})=M/(M\cap M^*)$, where $M^*$ is the conjugate of $M$ by any reflection in $W\setminus W^+$. It is trivial iff $\mathcal{P}$ is regular.

Problem. For each integer $k\ge 3$, define a group-theoretic invariant $X(\mathcal{P})$ (a generalized chirality, or irregularity, group) of a $k$-orbit abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ such that: (i) $X(\mathcal{P})$ is trivial if and only if $\mathcal{P}$ is regular; (ii) when $k=2$ and $\mathcal{P}$ is chiral, $X(\mathcal{P})$ recovers the classical chirality group $M/(M\cap M^*)$; (iii) the construction is intrinsic and does not depend on the choice of base flag, despite the fact that stabilizers in $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ of flags in different orbits need not be conjugate and may have non-conjugate normalizers; (iv) $X(\mathcal{P})$ quantifies how far $\mathcal{P}$ is from being regular and behaves functorially with respect to covers and quotients of $k$-orbit polytopes. Construct such an invariant and establish its basic properties.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is listed among open problems on $k$-orbit abstract polytopes. Subsequent literature on $k$-orbit polytopes characterizes their automorphism groups via symmetry type graphs but does not appear to provide a generally accepted "correct" generalization of the chirality group to $k$-orbit polytopes for $k\ge 3$. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Open problems on k-orbit polytopes
status_evidence.snippet: 35 open problems on combinatorial, geometric and algebraic aspects of k-orbit abstract polytopes.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as an open problem on k-orbit polytopes.

status_evidence.title: All polytopes are coset geometries: Characterizing automorphism groups of k-orbit abstract polytopes
status_evidence.snippet: A characterization of the automorphism group of a k-orbit polytope with given symmetry type graph can be given in terms of generators, relations and intersection conditions.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work characterizes k-orbit automorphism groups but does not define a generalized chirality group.

status_evidence.title: Chiral polytope - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: An abstract polytope of rank n is said to be chiral if its automorphism group has two orbits on the flags.
status_evidence.claim: The classical chirality group is currently only defined for 2-orbit chiral polytopes.
